title: What interoception is
objective: Define interoception and distinguish it from exteroception.

steps.title: Sensing inward
steps.body: **[[interoception|Interoception]]** is the nervous system's sense of the body's *internal* state — gut fullness, blood pressure, temperature, inflammation. It's distinct from **[[exteroception]]**, which senses the outside world (touch, sound, light). Interoception is mostly below awareness, and it drives reflexes and feelings alike.

steps.prompt: Which is an example of interoception rather than exteroception?
options: Feeling your stomach is full after a meal
Feeling the texture of a fabric with your fingertips
Hearing a door close down the hallway
Seeing a traffic light change to green
steps.explanation: Gut fullness is an internal-state signal (interoception). Fabric texture, sound and light are external stimuli (exteroception).

variants.setup: You're deciding which sense reports the body's internal state.
options: A fabric's texture under your fingertips
variants.reveal: Fullness is internal (interoception); fabric texture and sound are external (exteroception).

options: Below conscious awareness, yet they shape reflexes and feelings
Consciously felt most of the time, much as touch on the skin is
Used only to drive reflexes, with no influence on mood or feelings
Carried to the brain only by the vagus, never by spinal nerves
steps.explanation: You rarely 'feel' blood pressure or gut pH directly, yet these signals constantly drive autonomic reflexes and shape mood and 'gut feelings'. They reach the brain by both vagal and spinal routes.

variants.setup: Think about signals such as blood pressure, gut pH and blood glucose.
options: Reflex-only, with no effect on feelings
variants.reveal: They act largely unconsciously, yet steer reflexes and feelings.
